# Accessibility Overlay Over SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW

**Decision.** Draw the ACCEPT / MARGINAL / DECLINE bubble as a `TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY` window
attached to the already-running accessibility service, instead of a `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` "draw over
other apps" window.

**Date.** 2026-07-03, recorded in the CHANGELOG.

## The reason, as written

> "New `OverlayController.kt` draws the ACCEPT/MARGINAL/DECLINE bubble … using
> `TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY` (no extra permission; attached via the running service)."
> — Farley/docs/ocr-overlay/CHANGELOG.md, 2026-07-03

The whole argument is in the parenthesis. `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` is not a normal permission — it sends
the user out to a Settings screen for a scary-sounding grant, and it is the permission most associated
with overlay malware. `TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY` requires **no additional grant at all**, because the
service already holds the only permission that matters: `BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE`.

Onboarding cost was the deciding factor. The app already asks for the single most powerful grant on
Android ([[android-accessibility-service]]); adding a second alarming prompt on top of it is a real
chance of losing the user at setup, for a window that behaves the same either way.

## Alternative rejected

**`SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`** — the design originally documented in
`03-android-permissions-and-legal.md`. Rejected once the overlay was implemented, on the extra-grant
cost above. Nothing technical was lost: the bubble is `FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE` so it never steals input
from the ride app, tap-dismisses, and auto-hides after 20 s.

**The permission is still declared in the manifest.** `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` sits there unused, along
with `FOREGROUND_SERVICE` and `FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROJECTION` (fossils of the OCR path — see
[[node-tree-read-before-ocr]]) and `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` (no native location code). So the decision
achieved its goal in code and then failed to collect the benefit: a user or store reviewer inspecting
the manifest still sees the scary permission. Removing it was never done — and the permissions
chapter still documents the rejected design as the required one, an instance of
[[documentation-drift]].

## Second-order effect

Tying the overlay's lifetime to the service means the bubble cannot outlive the thing that produced it.
If the service is disabled, the window goes with it — there is no orphaned always-on-top view. For an
app whose overlay sits on top of another company's driver app while the user drives, that coupling is
a safety property, not just tidiness. It fits the restraint posture recorded on
[[never-automate-the-accept-tap]] and [[privacy-documented-beside-the-feature]].

## Never validated in the field

Like every native path in [[farely]], this ran in a debug build and never on a live shift. Whether the
overlay actually sits correctly over a Bolt offer card in traffic is untested — the state the roadmap
board honestly reports as "code-complete — remaining: validate on device". See [[phase-status-board]].
